task_context.problem_statement:
A subset of the integers $1,2,\cdots,100$ has the property that none of its members is 3 times another. What is the largest number of members such a subset can have?
$\text{(A) } 50\quad \text{(B) } 66\quad \text{(C) } 67\quad \text{(D) } 76\quad \text{(E) } 78$
task_context.reference_solution:
Notice that inclusion of the integers from $34$ to $100$ is allowed as long as no integer between $11$ and $33$ inclusive is within the set. This provides a total of $100 - 34 + 1$ = 67 solutions.
Further analyzation of the remaining integers between $1$ and $10$, we notice that we can include all the numbers except $3$ (as including $3$ would force us to remove both $9$ and $1$) to obtain the maximum number of $9$ solutions.
Thus, $67 + 9 = \boxed{76}$.

How far does that chain go before it exceeds 100?

Okay, so 1, 3, 9, 27, 81. That's 5 numbers. To make sure none is 3 times another, I can't pick two numbers that are next to each other in the chain. So I could pick 1, 9, and 81. That gives me 3 numbers from that chain. Do I do this for all the numbers?

That is a great way to look at it. Yes, every integer from 1 to 100 belongs to exactly one such chain. If you find the maximum number of elements you can pick from every possible chain without picking any two adjacent members, the sum of those maximums will be your answer.

Your observation about the range 34 to 100 is very helpful. It simplifies the process significantly. Now, instead of calculating every single chain, think about the numbers from 1 to 33. Which of those can you include without violating the rule, given that you've already included everything from 34 to 100?
